P1.evidence: P1a hit, and the only clean hit on this check in the batch — the rep signalled he had read the setter's notes and then proved it: 'So I went through everything that you told to my friend, Kaila. Yeah, there's a lot going on over there', followed by 'you have an experience of training twice a day, doing high rocks, all of stuff.' That is the check working as intended. P1b partial and thinner than his usual frame: 'I just want to understand where you're at right now and how we can actually potentially help you with', plus the takeaway, 'if there's an alignment, of course I can show you everything in granular. But if not, that's totally fine too.' Two of four parts — what you have tried and what you need were both absent. P1c partial: he tagged 'Yeah?' onto the frame and got 'Cool. Yeah', but never asked the explicit agreement question. P1d hit: 'brief me in your own words, like, what you're actually looking for.'

P2.evidence: Split down the middle: everything about training was asked well and everything about the person was skipped. P2a miss — no age, no height, no weight, on a fitness sale. P2b miss, and expensive: the rep learned the prospect travels constantly and has back-to-back meetings all day, asked where he was going (Mykonos, Ibiza, Saint-Tropez, Marbella) and never once asked what he does for a living. That is the ICP's occupation test, unasked, on the wealthiest prospect in the batch. P2c partial — injury questions were asked, but no general health or hereditary screen. P2d hit and well run: 'Any serious things?' produced the bilateral labral tears and stem cell treatment, 'Anything else that I need to know of?' produced the metal bar, eight screws and flat feet, and he followed up specifically — 'because you mentioned those shoulder injuries, do you have like stiffness in them?' Duration was not established, which is the only shortfall. P2e hit — the training week was mapped thoroughly: The Yard in the morning, gym in the afternoon, daily, plus 'Apart from gym, do you play any sports?' and 'do you have like a home gym, or do you have to come [to a gym]'. P2f hit — 'What's the biggest piece missing for you right now in terms of training that you do currently? Apart that you're bored with it' is exactly the results probe, and it produced the core and leg-day gaps. P2g hit — 'how about your diet? How does it look like? Is it dialed in or?', then the good follow-up 'is there an issue with that when you tend to fall off during travels?', which produced 'one bite turns into 20'. P2h and P2i miss — sleep and energy never raised, on a man training twice a day across time zones.

P3.evidence: The surface half ran and the deep half did not run at all, and that is the whole story of this call. P3a hit — 'Do you have, like, a specific goal with it that you want to achieve?' P3b hit and near-verbatim — 'if you would have to say like, would it be like getting stronger or like overall mobility type of thing?' produced mobility as the priority and core as the secondary. P3c partial — 'Any PRs that you want to hit?' is the nearest approach to something he wants and can't do; the answer was no and it was not pursued. P3d, P3e, P3f and P3g are all misses and there is no partial credit available: the bridge question was never asked in any form, no version of 'outside of the physical, what's actually driving this' appeared, nobody was ever asked what moving better would do for him, nobody was asked who else it impacts, and nothing was driven through to family, identity, legacy or longevity. The rep did not establish this man's age, occupation, or whether he has a partner or children. The entire conversation stayed on logistics: travel, equipment and boredom. P3h partial — there were reflect-backs, but only of surface facts: 'So basically, you're looking for something that you could implement into your workouts when you're traveling, right?' and 'So mobility would be the baseline for you and the foundation.' The consequence is direct and traceable: with nothing emotional ever attached to the purchase, the prospect's own summary of what he was buying became 'In my mind, what I want is just a program' — which is exactly what a call that never left the logistics layer produces.

P4.evidence: P4a partial — current training was mapped in detail but past attempts were never asked about; the Barry's-style classes surfaced on their own. P4b and P4c miss, and this is the costly pair. The prospect volunteered his own failure pattern in one sentence — 'eventually I just got so bored of it. I couldn't go anymore' — and he is currently sitting in the same pattern with a gym routine he is 'just over'. Boredom-driven abandonment is his root cause, it appeared twice unprompted, and the rep asked nothing about it either time. P4d partial — 'What's the biggest piece missing for you right now in terms of training that you do currently?' is a gap question, but it produced preferences (core, leg day) rather than structure. P4e miss — no structural gap was ever named. P4f miss, and it went beyond omission into self-harm: rather than asking why he cannot sustain this on his own, the rep asked him to confirm that he can — 'And the third part, you said that you don't need hand-holding. Is that correct?' The prospect agreed, and the accountability case was surrendered before it was made.

P5.evidence: Not run in any form. No cost of inaction, no two-year question, no settling question, no line in the sand. There was material available — a plateau he is frustrated by, four labral tears held together by stem cell injections, a rodded leg, and a documented history of quitting things from boredom — and none of it was turned into a consequence. Without Phase 5 the price had nothing to sit against, which is why the conversation moved straight from the number to a negotiation about scope.

P6.evidence: P6a miss — the belief question was never asked. P6b partial — two soft temperature checks stood in for it: 'So how do you feel about overall?' and 'So does it sound like you want to do it, or like, eh?' Neither is the scripted go-all-in question and neither surfaces hidden blockers. P6c miss, and clearly so. The answer to 'does it sound like you want to do it' was not a yes, it was a question — 'if I say yes, is it just like, I get a full program, or like, just curious how it works, and what the price is, I guess?' The rep proceeded to deliverables and then to the number anyway, and never returned to Phase 5 when the scope objection landed. He had also, minutes earlier, been told the accountability pillar was unwanted, which is the clearest possible signal to go back rather than forward.

P11.evidence: P11a is scored a miss rather than N/A because the moment became live and was not taken. After the rep proposed the 30-day trial, the prospect said 'Yeah, I think that would work', and after the rep confirmed the price the prospect said 'Okay, cool.' At that point payment should have been requested. Instead the rep re-explained the trial and accepted 'let me just check a few other things and then I will get back to you.' No card was asked for, no link was mentioned, and the deal was pushed to Friday. P11b, P11c and P11d are N/A: with no payment taken, the Trevor onboarding booking, the agreement signature and the welcome-email walkthrough were unreachable.

objection_plays.detail: Triggered twice. On the first ('I'll think on it. I'll let you guys know') the rep ran the single best move in the play and ran it well: 'So what's coming up for you right now that's keeping you from actually moving forward?' It worked — it produced a specific, actionable answer rather than a stall, 'I just don't know, for me personally, if me spending $4,000 on this makes sense.' He then stopped running the play and started building product instead. Not run at any point: 'do you feel what we've gone through CAN get you to [goal]', 'what makes you feel it can', 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here — when do you make a different decision', 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now', and the closing 'are you sure? Nothing else keeping you from being 100% in?' On the second trigger, twenty seconds after the prospect had said the trial would work, the rep granted the delay outright with no play at all.

Recorded deliberately as a non-trigger, because it superficially looks like a money objection and is not. The prospect ruled money out himself, unprompted and emphatically: 'it's not even like the $4,000. I spend way more on stupid [stuff] all the time', against a disclosed baseline of $1,500-$2,000 a month on personal trainers. Running the open-wallet play here — asking for cash on hand, credit cards, available credit — would have been both wrong and insulting. The rep correctly did not run it, and that judgement deserves credit. The problem is what he ran instead: having correctly diagnosed that price was not the barrier, he responded by cutting the price three times.

SCRIPT GAP, and a new one — value at reduced scope. The prospect does not want the offer; he wants a third of it. 'I'd rather just pay for a program is really where my head's at, more so than paying for an ongoing handholding', and then plainly, 'what I want is not necessarily something that you guys normally sell. Like, I just want to buy a program.' None of the five plays addresses a prospect who accepts the value, can afford the price, and rejects the scope. The rep tried one rebuttal — that a kettlebell novice needs the coaching layer — and when the prospect conceded month one and refused the rest, the counter was a single line: 'Well, you will learn the basics throughout the month, and then you will progress, right?' He then stopped arguing and started discounting. Scored partial for the attempted rebuttal. A real play is needed here, and it should probably be built on the prospect's own failure pattern — this is a man who quits things when he gets bored, which is an argument for check-ins, not against them, and it was sitting in the transcript unused.

SECOND SCRIPT GAP — in-person versus virtual value. 'I spend 1,500, 2K a month sometimes on trainers when I'm here... to spend the same amount for virtual seems a little crazy.' The rep asked the right opening question, 'What's so crazy about it?', which is exactly how to attack an unexamined assumption, and then dropped it when the answer came back soft ('just a different experience in my mind'). No play exists for the modality objection, and it is the one that matters most for a premium remote offer sold to people who already buy in-person training. The unused counter was on the table: this prospect travels roughly half the year, and an in-person trainer in Los Angeles does not exist in Mykonos.

THIRD SCRIPT GAP — free online resources, the third appearance of this shape in this batch. 'For what I want, and all the online resources and things, like, it just seems silly for me to spend so much money on.' Unlike the other two occurrences, here it drew no response whatsoever; the rep said 'Okay. I get it' and pivoted to proposing the trial. Logging it because the frequency now matters: three of the four sales calls in this batch were partly or wholly lost to a free alternative, and the playbook has nothing for it.

notes: The clearest example in the batch of good front-of-call work being wasted by skipping the middle. Genuine strengths: the only real read-back of setter notes anywhere in this batch, thorough injury and training-history questioning, an accurate read that money was not the objection, and one well-run Objection A move that produced a specific blocker instead of a stall. Then everything that creates willingness to pay was skipped — the whole deep half of Phase 3, all of Phase 4's root cause, all of Phase 5, and any real commitment check — so when the number landed there was nothing holding it up. Two moments to coach specifically. First, at 00:14:26 the rep asked the prospect to confirm he did not need the accountability pillar before presenting it; that single question surrendered a third of the offer and became the prospect's central objection six minutes later. Second, on being told the scope was wrong, the rep cut price three times in four minutes — $6,000, then $4,000, then an invented $1,500 30-day trial he named 'love it or leave it' on the spot — and then, when the prospect agreed to the trial, did not ask for payment. Escalate the pricing separately from the coaching: the $4,000 three-month tier is not in the documented offer and this rep has now quoted it twice in three days, and the 30-day trial appears to have been created live with no terms, one day after his manager told him longer or non-standard payment structures are 'not generally an option that we offer' while also telling him to get creative if he needed to get a deal through.
